claim.hypothesis: At the level of U.S.counties,support for Donald Trump in the 2016 presidential election will be negatively associated with social distancing behavior.
claim.hypothesis_location: The hypothesis is not stated explicitly in the text but the relationship is mentioned in the abstract, introduction and results sections.
claim.statement: An interquartile increase in support for Trump (I.Q.R. = 20.3%) resulted in a 4.1 percentage point decrease in social distancing (95% C.I. = 3.0–5.2) [ p < 0.001].

original_results.summary: An interquartile increase in support for Trump (20.3%) was associated with a 4.1-percentage-point decrease in social distancing (95% CI = 3.0–5.2, p < 0.001).

human_result_summary: Human team (Tyner/Huntington-Klein/Fox, COS): county-level regression with state fixed effects, n=3076; Share of Trump Voters coefficient -0.078 (SE 0.018), p=.000015. Scaled per one IQR of Trump share: -1.59 pp of social distancing vs -4.1 pp in the original, so same sign and significant but a notably smaller effect ('consistent but of reduced size'). Report's verdict: replicates the original result.

tolerance.note: Replicated = same sign, statistically significant at the paper's threshold, and effect size in the same ballpark as the human report.
